18. I have considered the submissions and combed through evidence on record very carefully.
19. The ld. Addl. PP for the State has argued that guilt of accused persons has been proved on record and they may be FIR No. 10/2012 State Vs. Ashu & Ors.
PS Mandawali Page no. 12 of 22  convicted charges.
On the other hand, ld. defence counsel argued that prosecution witnesses did not support the case of prosecution.
The prosecution has failed to establish the guilt of accused persons beyond reasonable doubt.
Hence, all the accused may be acquitted.

20. Before adverting to the appreciation of evidence on record, it is observed that Section 304B IPC is distinct from the other penal provisions of the Code in as much as it shifts the burden upon the accused to dislodge the 'presumption' that such person had caused the dowry death of the victim.

In other words, Section 304B IPC read with Section 113B of Indian Evidence Act raises a presumption as to commission of dowry death of a woman if it is 'shown' that soon before her death, such woman was subjected by accused to cruelty or harassment for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry.
The aforesaid burden cast upon the accused is not only onerous but also lowers the standard of proof required from the prosecution to prove the commission of offence of dowry death.

21. While dealing with the aforesaid issue of 'presumption' and 'burden of proof' in a case of dowry death, the Hon'ble Supreme Court, while discussing the jurisprudence on the subject, in case titled Sher Singh @ Partapa vs State Of Haryana AIR 2015 SC CRI 481 observed as under :-
9.

sentences.text: Death can be accidental, suicidal or homicidal.

The first type is a tragedy and no criminal complexion is conjured up, unless statutorily so devised, as in Section 304A;
but even there the culpable act is that of the person actually causing the death.

It seems to us that Section 304B of the IPC, inasmuch as it also takes within its contemplation "the FIR No. 10/2012 State Vs. Ashu & Ors.
PS Mandawali Page no. 13 of 22 death of a woman ..... otherwise than under normal circumstances", endeavours to cover murders masquerading as accidents.

Justifiably,
the suicidal death of a married woman who was meted out with cruelty by her husband, where her demise occurred within seven years of marriage in connection State vs Ashu on 29 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22535978/

sentences.text:
In Section 113A of the Evidence Act Parliament has, in the case of a wife's suicide,
"presumed" the guilt of the husband and the members of his family.
Significantly, in Section 113B which pointedly refers to dowry deaths, Parliament has again employed the word "presume".
However, in substantially similar circumstances, in the event of a wife's unnatural death, Parliament has in Section 304B "deemed" the guilt of the husband and the members of his family.

The Concise Oxford Dictionary defines the word "presume" as: supposed to be true, take for granted; whereas "deem" as: regard,
consider; and whereas "show" as:
point out and prove.

The Concise Dictionary of Law, Oxford Paperbacks has this comprehensive yet succinct definition of burden of proof which is worthy of reproduction:
"Burden of Proof: The duty of a party to litigation to prove a fact or facts in issue.

Generally the burden of proof falls upon the party FIR No. 10/2012 State Vs. Ashu &
Ors.
PS Mandawali Page no. 14 of 22 who substantially asserts the truth of a particular fact (the prosecution or the plaintiff).

sentences.text: A distinction is drawn between the persuasive (or legal) burden, which is carried by the party who as a matter of law will lose the case if he fails to prove the fact in issue; and the evidential burden (burden of adducing evidence or burden of going forward), which is the duty of showing that there is sufficient evidence to raise an issue fit for the consideration of the trier of fact as to the existence or non-existence of a fact in issue.

The normal rule is that a defendant is presumed to be innocent until he is proved guilty; it is therefore the duty of the prosecution to prove its case by establishing both the actus reus of the crime and the mens rea.
It must first satisfy the evidential burden to show that its allegations have something to support them.
If it cannot satisfy this burden, the defence may submit or the judge may direct that there is no case to answer, and the judge must direct the jury to acquit.

The prosecution may State vs Ashu on 29 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22535978/
8 sometimes rely on presumptions of fact to satisfy the evidential burden of proof (e.g.
the fact that a woman was subjected to violence during sexual intercourse will normally raise a presumption to support a charge of rape and prove that she did not consent).

If, however, the prosecution has established a basis for its case, it must then continue to satisfy the persuasive burden by proving its case beyond reasonable doubt (see proof beyond reasonable doubt).

It is the duty of the judge to tell the jury clearly that the prosecution must prove its case and that it must prove it beyond reasonable doubt; if he does not give this clear direction, the defendant is entitled to be acquitted.

14. As is already noted above, Section 113B of the Evidence Act and Section 304B of the IPC were introduced into their respective statutes simultaneously and, therefore,
it must ordinarily be assumed that Parliament intentionally used the word 'deemed'
in Section 304B to distinguish this provision from the others.
In actuality, however, it is well nigh impossible to give a sensible and legally acceptable meaning to these FIR No. 10/2012 State Vs. Ashu & Ors.
PS Mandawali Page no. 15 of 22 provisions, unless the word 'shown' is used as synonymous to 'prove' and the word 'presume' as freely interchangeable with the word 'deemed'.

In the realm of civil and fiscal law, it is not difficult to import the ordinary meaning of the word 'deem' to denote a set of circumstances which call to be construed contrary to what they actually are.
In criminal legislation, however, it is unpalatable to adopt this approach by rote.

We have the high authority of the Constitution Bench of this Court both in State of Travancore-Cochin v. Shanmugha Vilas Cashewnut Factory AIR 1953 SC 333 and State of Tamil Nadu v. Arooran Sugars Limited (1997) 1 SCC 326, requiring the Court to ascertain the purpose behind the statutory fiction brought about by the use of the word 'deemed' so as to give full effect to the legislation and carry it to its logical conclusion.

sentences.text: We may add that it is generally posited that there are rebuttable as well as irrebuttable presumptions, the latter oftentimes assuming an artificiality as actuality by means of a deeming provision.
It is abhorrent to criminal jurisprudence to adjudicate a person guilty of an offence even though he had neither intention to commit it nor active participation in its commission.
It is after deep cogitation that we consider it imperative to construe the word 'shown' in Section 304B of the IPC as to, in fact, connote 'prove'.

In other words, it is for the prosecution to prove that a 'dowry death' has occurred, namely, (i)
that the death of a woman has been caused in abnormal circumstances by her having been burned or having been bodily injured, (ii) within seven years of a marriage, (iii)
and that she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband, (iv) in connection with any demand for dowry and (v) that the cruelty or harassment meted out to her continued to have a causal connection or a live link with the demand of dowry.

We are aware that the word 'soon' finds place in Section 304B; but we would prefer to interpret its use not in terms of days or months or years, but as necessarily indicating that the demand for dowry should not be stale or an aberration of the past, but should be the continuing cause for the death under State vs Ashu on 29 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22535978/
9 Section 304B or the suicide under FIR No. 10/2012 State Vs. Ashu & Ors.
PS Mandawali Page no. 16 of 22 Section 306 of the IPC. Once the presence of these concomitants are established or shown or proved by the prosecution, even by preponderance of possibility, the initial presumption of innocence is replaced by an assumption of guilt of the accused, thereupon transferring the heavy burden of proof upon him and requiring him to produce evidence dislodging his guilt, beyond reasonable doubt.

sentences.text: It seems to us that what Parliament intended by using the word 'deemed' was that only preponderance of evidence would be insufficient to discharge the husband or his family members of their guilt.
This interpretation provides the accused a chance of proving their innocence.
This is also the postulation of Section 101 of the Evidence Act.

The purpose of Section 113B of the Evidence Act and Section 304B of the IPC, in our opinion, is to counter what is commonly encountered - the lack or the absence of evidence in the case of suicide or death of a woman within seven years of marriage.

If the word "shown" has to be given its ordinary meaning then it would only require the prosecution to merely present its evidence in Court,
not necessarily through oral deposition, and thereupon make the accused lead detailed evidence to be followed by that of the prosecution.

This procedure is unknown to Common Law systems, and beyond the contemplation of the Cr.P.C.
17.....

Therefore, the burden of proof weighs on the husband to prove his innocence by dislodging his deemed culpability, and that this has to be preceded only by the prosecution proving the presence of three factors, viz. (i) the death of a woman in abnormal circumstances (ii) within seven years of her marriage, and (iii) and that the death had a live link with cruelty connected with any demand of dowry.
The other facet is that the husband has indeed a heavy burden cast on his shoulders in that his deemed culpability would have to be displaced and overturned beyond reasonable doubt.
...It is also important to highlight that Section 304B does not require the accused to give evidence against himself but casts the onerous burden to dislodge his deemed guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

In our FIR No. 10/2012 State Vs. Ashu & Ors.
PS Mandawali Page no. 17 of 22 opinion, it would not be appropriate to lessen the husband's onus to that of preponderance of probability as that would annihilate the deemed guilt expressed in Section 304B, and such a curial interpretation would defeat and neutralise the intentions and purposes of Parliament.

sentences.text: A scenario which readily comes to mind is where dowry demands have indubitably been made by the accused husband, where in an agitated state of mind, the wife had decided to leave her matrimonial home, and where while travelling by bus to her parents' home she sustained fatal burn injuries in an accident/collision which that bus encountered.
Surely, if the husband proved that he played no role whatsoever in the accident, he could not be deemed to have caused his wife's death.

It needs to be immediately clarified that if the wife had taken her life by jumping in front of a bus or before a State vs Ashu on 29 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22535978/
10 train, the husband would have no defence.
Examples can be legion, and hence we shall abjure from going any further.

All that needs to be said is that if the husband proves facts which portray, beyond reasonable doubt, that he could not have caused the death of his wife by burns or bodily injury or not involved in any manner in her death in abnormal circumstances, he would not be culpable under Section 304B.
19.
We must consider, lastly, whether the prosecution has successfully 'shown' that the deceased was subjected to cruelty which was connected with dowry demands.
We may usefully reiterate here that keeping in perspective the use of "shown" instead of "proved" the onus would stand satisfied on the anvil of preponderance of evidence.

22 ...What motivated or compelled her to take this extreme and horrific step will remain a mystery, as we are not satisfied that the prosecution has proved or even shown that she was treated with such cruelty, connected with dowry demands, as led her to commit suicide.

In the normal course dowry demands are articulated when the marriage is agreed upon and is certainly reiterated at the time when it is performed and such demands continue into a couple of years of matrimony.
In normal course, if a woman is being tortured and harassed, she would not remain FIR No. 10/2012 State Vs. Ashu & Ors.
PS Mandawali Page no. 18 of 22 reticent of this state of affairs and would certainly repeatedly inform her family. This is specially so before she takes the extreme step of taking her own life.
Added to this are the inconsistencies and contradictions between the statements of PW4 and PW7 with regard to the panchayat and the presence of and knowledge of Gurdip Singh.

It is for these reasons that we are of the opinion that the prosecution has not shown/presented and or proved even by preponderance of probabilities that the deceased had been treated with cruelty emanating from or founded on dowry demands...."

22. Being guided by the aforesaid precedent, the Court shall first examine the testimony of material public witnesses and thereafter, shall make an attempt to reconcile the allegations in their testimonies and analyze if prosecution succeeded in bringing home the guilt of accused persons.
23. The case of prosecution is that the deceased Shashi had committed suicide by hanging due to harassment caused to her by accused person for not bringing dowry.

Perusal of postmortem examination report of deceased Ex. PW1/A and the opinion regarding cause of death given by PW-1 Dr. B. N. Acharya Ex. PW1/B has established that deceased had committed suicide by hanging herself from the ceiling fan.

However, the case of prosecution rested on the testimonies of parents of deceased i.e. PW-3 Maya Devi and PW-4 Rambir to bring home the allegations of harassment caused to her with respect to demand of dowry.
24. PW-3 Maya Devi and PW-4 Rambir

in their original statements recorded by SDM i.e. Ex. PW3/B and Ex. PW4/B had alleged that accused persons used to harass their daughter Shashi for not fulfilling their demand of bringing cash in dowry.

wherein she alleged that the police was not conducting fair investigation.

However, in their examinations in chief both the parents of deceased i.e. PW-3 Maya Devi and PW-4 Rambir categorically stated that accused persons had never demanded any dowry or money from their daughter or from them.
They also deposed that their daughter Shashi was kept well in her matrimonial house.
25. PW-3 Maya Devi and PW-4 Rambir were cross- examined at length by ld. PP for the State.
In her cross- examination, PW-3 Maya Devi stated that she had not stated to SDM that accused persons used to beat her daughter or used to demand dowry from her.
She also denied her statement showing apprehension that accused persons had killed her daughter Shashi.
She also denied the remaining averments of her statement Ex. PW3/B.
Similarly, PW-4 Ramir Singh in his cross-examination also denied the suggestion that SDM had recorded his statement on his narration.
He also denied having alleged that her daughter was given beatings by accused persons or they used to demand dowry from her.
In his cross-examination he stated that at the time of death of her daughter he was not in fit state of mind and did not know whether SDM had recorded the contents of what he had stated to him.

26. Thus, perusal of depositions of parents of deceased show that they completely disowned the case of prosecution vis-a- vis demand of dowry and harassment caused to their daughter by accused persons.
FIR No. 10/2012 State Vs. Ashu & Ors.
PS Mandawali Page no. 20 of 22 27.
The prosecution also alleged that previously deceased had lodged a police complaint against accused person with allegations of harassment on account of demand of dowry.
It is the case of prosecution that FIR no. 636/2008 of PS Atrauli u/s 323/498-A/34 IPC was registered against accused persons.
However, at the same time, investigating officer himself filed a copy of judgment passed by the court in the aforesaid case, whereby all accused were acquitted.
Perusal of aforesaid judgment Ex. C1 shows that the complainant Shashi (now deceased) had deposed that accused persons neither made demand of dowry nor they had harassed her.

28. Thus, the basic ingredients of the offence of dowry death i.e. cruelty or harassment of the victim for or in connection with the demand for dowry soon before her death, remained elusive to the case of prosecution.

As laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sher Singh (Supra), when the prosecution failed to prove its case against the accused persons even on the standard of preponderance of probabilities, to show the existence of basic ingredients of offence, the 'presumption' provided under Section 113B Indian Evidence Act would remain in-operational and can not play out against the accused.
In other words, accused can not be held guilty merely on the basis of statutory presumption.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In other words, Section 304B IPC read with Section 113B of Indian Evidence Act raises a presumption as to commission of dowry death of a woman if it is 'shown' that soon before her death, such woman was subjected by accused to cruelty or harassment for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry.
The aforesaid burden cast upon the accused is not only onerous but also lowers the standard of proof required from the prosecution to prove the commission of offence of dowry death.
Justifiably,
the suicidal death of a married woman who was meted out with cruelty by her husband, where her demise occurred within seven years of marriage in connection State vs Ashu on 29 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22535978/
7 with a dowry demand should lead to prosecution and punishment under Sections 304B and/or 306 of the IPC.
However, if the perfidious harassment and cruelty by the husband is conclusively proved by him to have had no causal connection with his cruel behaviour based on a dowry demand, these provisions are not attracted as held in Bhagwan Das v. Kartar Singh (2007) 11 SCC 205, although some reservation may remain regarding the reach of Section 306.
13.
In Section 113A of the Evidence Act Parliament has, in the case of a wife's suicide,
"presumed" the guilt of the husband and the members of his family.
A distinction is drawn between the persuasive (or legal) burden, which is carried by the party who as a matter of law will lose the case if he fails to prove the fact in issue; and the evidential burden (burden of adducing evidence or burden of going forward), which is the duty of showing that there is sufficient evidence to raise an issue fit for the consideration of the trier of fact as to the existence or non-existence of a fact in issue.
The normal rule is that a defendant is presumed to be innocent until he is proved guilty; it is therefore the duty of the prosecution to prove its case by establishing both the actus reus of the crime and the mens rea.
It must first satisfy the evidential burden to show that its allegations have something to support them.
If it cannot satisfy this burden, the defence may submit or the judge may direct that there is no case to answer, and the judge must direct the jury to acquit.
If, however, the prosecution has established a basis for its case, it must then continue to satisfy the persuasive burden by proving its case beyond reasonable doubt (see proof beyond reasonable doubt).
It is the duty of the judge to tell the jury clearly that the prosecution must prove its case and that it must prove it beyond reasonable doubt; if he does not give this clear direction, the defendant is entitled to be acquitted.
In actuality, however, it is well nigh impossible to give a sensible and legally acceptable meaning to these FIR No. 10/2012 State Vs. Ashu & Ors.
PS Mandawali Page no. 15 of 22 provisions, unless the word 'shown' is used as synonymous to 'prove' and the word 'presume' as freely interchangeable with the word 'deemed'.
In the realm of civil and fiscal law, it is not difficult to import the ordinary meaning of the word 'deem' to denote a set of circumstances which call to be construed contrary to what they actually are.
In criminal legislation, however, it is unpalatable to adopt this approach by rote.
We have the high authority of the Constitution Bench of this Court both in State of Travancore-Cochin v. Shanmugha Vilas Cashewnut Factory AIR 1953 SC 333 and State of Tamil Nadu v. Arooran Sugars Limited (1997) 1 SCC 326, requiring the Court to ascertain the purpose behind the statutory fiction brought about by the use of the word 'deemed' so as to give full effect to the legislation and carry it to its logical conclusion.
We may add that it is generally posited that there are rebuttable as well as irrebuttable presumptions, the latter oftentimes assuming an artificiality as actuality by means of a deeming provision.
It is abhorrent to criminal jurisprudence to adjudicate a person guilty of an offence even though he had neither intention to commit it nor active participation in its commission.
It is after deep cogitation that we consider it imperative to construe the word 'shown' in Section 304B of the IPC as to, in fact, connote 'prove'.
In other words, it is for the prosecution to prove that a 'dowry death' has occurred, namely, (i)
that the death of a woman has been caused in abnormal circumstances by her having been burned or having been bodily injured, (ii) within seven years of a marriage, (iii)
and that she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband, (iv) in connection with any demand for dowry and (v) that the cruelty or harassment meted out to her continued to have a causal connection or a live link with the demand of dowry.
We are aware that the word 'soon' finds place in Section 304B; but we would prefer to interpret its use not in terms of days or months or years, but as necessarily indicating that the demand for dowry should not be stale or an aberration of the past, but should be the continuing cause for the death under State vs Ashu on 29 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22535978/
9 Section 304B or the suicide under FIR No. 10/2012 State Vs. Ashu & Ors.
PS Mandawali Page no. 16 of 22 Section 306 of the IPC. Once the presence of these concomitants are established or shown or proved by the prosecution, even by preponderance of possibility, the initial presumption of innocence is replaced by an assumption of guilt of the accused, thereupon transferring the heavy burden of proof upon him and requiring him to produce evidence dislodging his guilt, beyond reasonable doubt.
It seems to us that what Parliament intended by using the word 'deemed' was that only preponderance of evidence would be insufficient to discharge the husband or his family members of their guilt.
The purpose of Section 113B of the Evidence Act and Section 304B of the IPC, in our opinion, is to counter what is commonly encountered - the lack or the absence of evidence in the case of suicide or death of a woman within seven years of marriage.
If the word "shown" has to be given its ordinary meaning then it would only require the prosecution to merely present its evidence in Court,
not necessarily through oral deposition, and thereupon make the accused lead detailed evidence to be followed by that of the prosecution.
A scenario which readily comes to mind is where dowry demands have indubitably been made by the accused husband, where in an agitated state of mind, the wife had decided to leave her matrimonial home, and where while travelling by bus to her parents' home she sustained fatal burn injuries in an accident/collision which that bus encountered.
As laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sher Singh (Supra), when the prosecution failed to prove its case against the accused persons even on the standard of preponderance of probabilities, to show the existence of basic ingredients of offence, the 'presumption' provided under Section 113B Indian Evidence Act would remain in-operational and can not play out against the accused.
In other words, accused can not be held guilty merely on the basis of statutory presumption.
In the opinion of this Court, the benefit of doubt in the case of prosecution created on account of deficient evidence of the witnesses, must be accorded to both the accused.
